reference.source: British Committee for Standards in Haematology / Cairo-Bishop tumour lysis guidance
clinicalPearls: Defined by the Cairo-Bishop criteria as laboratory TLS (two or more of hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia within a defined window) progressing to clinical TLS when renal impairment, arrhythmia, seizure or death supervene.

Highest risk with bulky, rapidly proliferating and chemosensitive malignancies: Burkitt and other high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphomas, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, and acute leukaemias with high white-cell counts or high LDH.

Spontaneous TLS may occur before any cytotoxic therapy (classically Burkitt lymphoma) and characteristically shows hyperuricaemia without the hyperphosphataemia typical of treatment-induced TLS, because released phosphate is reincorporated into new tumour cells.

Secondary hypocalcaemia results from calcium-phosphate precipitation; give calcium only for symptomatic hypocalcaemia because supplementation risks metastatic calcification and worsening acute kidney injury.

Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) rapidly degrades existing urate and is preferred for high-risk or established TLS; it is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency owing to the risk of haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia.
Allopurinol or febuxostat prevents new urate formation but does not lower an existing urate load, so it is a prophylactic (not rescue) agent in lower-risk patients.

Aggressive isotonic intravenous fluid to maintain a high urine output is the cornerstone; routine urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended because it promotes calcium-phosphate deposition in the kidney.

Early nephrology involvement and low threshold for renal replacement therapy are warranted for refractory hyperkalaemia, symptomatic hypocalcaemia with hyperphosphataemia, volume overload or oligoanuric acute kidney injury.
reference.pathophysiology: Rapid lysis of a large, proliferative tumour burden—either spontaneously or precipitated by cytotoxic therapy, corticosteroids or radiotherapy—releases intracellular potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids into the circulation faster than renal excretion can clear them. Purine catabolism generates uric acid that precipitates in the distal tubules and collecting ducts, while hyperphosphataemia drives calcium-phosphate crystal deposition; both cause intrarenal obstruction, vasoconstriction and inflammation leading to acute kidney injury, which in turn compounds the metabolic derangement. The resulting hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia produce the cardiac and neuromuscular complications that define clinical TLS.
additionalDifferentials: Acute kidney injury from sepsis, nephrotoxins or contrast
Pre-existing chronic kidney disease with electrolyte derangement
Pseudohyperkalaemia from sample haemolysis or extreme leucocytosis
Primary hyperphosphataemia from exogenous phosphate administration
additionalInvestigations: Serial urea, electrolytes and creatinine with urate, phosphate, calcium and magnesium
Lactate dehydrogenase and uric acid to gauge tumour burden and risk
Twelve-lead ECG for hyperkalaemic changes and QT prolongation from hypocalcaemia
Venous or arterial blood gas for acid-base status
Strict fluid balance and hourly urine output monitoring
G6PD assay before rasburicase where clinically feasible
Full blood count and coagulation screen to detect concurrent DIC or leukostasis
redFlags: ECG changes or arrhythmia from severe hyperkalaemia
Tetany, carpopedal spasm or seizures from acute hypocalcaemia
Oliguria or anuria signalling established acute kidney injury
Rapidly rising potassium or phosphate despite fluids
reference.prognosis: With pre-emptive risk stratification, hydration and urate-lowering therapy most cases are preventable or reversible, but established clinical TLS with acute kidney injury carries significant morbidity and mortality. Outcome depends on early recognition, control of the underlying malignancy and timely renal support.
pitfalls: Administering intravenous calcium for asymptomatic hypocalcaemia, precipitating calcium-phosphate deposition
Relying on allopurinol to treat an already elevated urate load instead of using rasburicase
Giving rasburicase without excluding G6PD deficiency
Continuing urinary alkalinisation, which worsens calcium-phosphate precipitation
Misinterpreting spurious hyperkalaemia from a haemolysed or delayed sample and either over- or under-treating
references: Cairo MS, Bishop M. Tumour lysis syndrome: classification and consensus grading
British Committee for Standards in Haematology guideline on management of tumour lysis syndrome
